What are the main differences and similarities between Sunni-Shia fights compared to wars between Catholics and Protestants a few centuries ago?
The biggest difference I see is that the Sunni and Shia are still fighting.

The Catholic reformation movement which led to the creation of Protestantism happened about 1500 years after Catholicism and what we'd generally call Christianity was invented. Christianity was still in its convert-or-kill phase, but it was moving away from it. The final Christian crusade, which received little support, was called in the same century that the schism that would become Protestantism was growing. The Sunni/Shia split on the other hand happened immediately after Muhammad died and Islam was just starting to get warmed up in its convert-or-kill phase. So you have centuries of two groups killing and defiling each other at every possible opportunity.

The Sunni-Shia split also happened in the 'magic phase' of the religion. When people think of Christianity there's the magic phase of resurrections, water to wine, walking on water, and so on. And then there's the human phase of things like institutional churches, beatifications, and so on. The main difference is time. Religious folks tend to be more willing to suspend disbelief, consciously or not, for events as long as they happened sufficiently long ago and were written down on paper by somebody that said he talked to god(s). If somebody long enough ago says the man turned water into wine, then the man turned water into wine - period. By contrast people are far more skeptical of things like the church's actions that happened 1000+ years as the magic phase had long since passed. But the Sunni-Shia split, happening right after the death of Muhammad, puts it right in the magic zone where people who adopt either side are going to be more inclined to simply accept without doubt. Your religion says you're right and the other side must die then you're right and the other side must die - period.

A general consideration is that support for local beliefs also thrive in the presence of an apparently unjustified real and direct foreign threat to those beliefs. When your religion or religiosity is unjustly attacked by perceived outsiders it's going to strengthen your resolve. And both sides of the Sunni-Shia split see the other side as basically saying, "You're wrong. Die!" Whereas the Protestant split had a large number of justifiable reasons including increasingly visible corruption within the establishment church.

This is pure and original speculation on my part. I'm certainly no religious scholar, but I think it's an interesting question.
